claims.claim: The classic definition of culture in anthropology comes from nineteenth-century British anthropologist Edward Burnett Tylor, who in Primitive Culture (1871) described culture as 'that complex whole which includes knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom, and any other capabilities and habits acquired by man as a member of society.'

OpenStax's Introduction to Anthropology describes culture as the whole way of life of a society, combining material objects, technologies, social relationships, everyday practices, deeply held values, and shared ideas, and treats culture as the central concept uniting all four fields of anthropology.

No single definition of culture ever won universal agreement: in Culture: A Critical Review of Concepts and Definitions (1952), anthropologists A. L. Kroeber and Clyde Kluckhohn cited 164 published definitions of culture, ranging from 'learned behavior' to 'ideas in the mind.'

Culture is learned, not inherited: acquired behaviors are cultural, innate behaviors are biological, and cultural knowledge is passed between people through the process of enculturation rather than through genes.

Culture is shared: for an element of behavior to count as cultural, both the action and its meaning must be commonly known among members of a group; individual habits are not culture until a group learns and recognizes them.

Culture is symbolic: a symbol is an object, image, or gesture conventionally associated with a particular meaning, and symboling is the human capacity to assign meanings that cannot be grasped with the senses alone (e.g., the meaning of the word 'dog' is assigned, not inherent in the sound).

Culture is integrated: culture is a combination of materials, technologies, social relationships, practices, values, and ideas whose parts fit together, so a change in one element ripples through the others (the holistic view).

Culture is dynamic: culture is continuous but changes, and the four main mechanisms of cultural change are diffusion (movement of an element between societies), friction (conflict between elements), innovation (slight alteration of an existing element), and invention (creation of a new element); Franz Boas argued cultural elements are highly mobile through trade and migration.

Culture is shared but also contested and uneven: different members and subgroups of a society hold different versions of and perspectives on their common culture, so no single member can fully represent a whole culture.

Culture typically feels familiar and natural to the people inside it — OpenStax calls this the 'homeyness' of culture — which is why people usually notice their own culture mainly when they encounter a setting where its assumptions no longer hold.

positions: Britannica's article (following Leslie A. White) presents culture as behaviour peculiar to Homo sapiens, dependent on the capacity for symboling.
The same Britannica article concedes that socially transmitted behavioral traditions — patterns of behavior passed by social rather than biological means — have been documented in nonhuman animals.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson does not claim culture is unique to humans. It uses the two-part test anthropologists apply (learned and shared) and describes culture as the system by which human groups live, which is what the OpenStax textbook chapter actually teaches. The uniqueness question is flagged as an open scholarly debate, not asserted.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which definition of culture should a lesson teach?
positions: Tylor's 1871 definition ('that complex whole...') is treated as the classic definition by both OpenStax and Britannica.
Kroeber and Kluckhohn (1952) catalogued 164 competing definitions, and some scholars have argued the concept is too contradictory to keep at all (OpenStax 3.6).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches a working definition (learned, shared system of beliefs, practices, and meanings of a group) alongside Tylor's classic definition and the OpenStax description, and states honestly that hundreds of definitions exist. It presents the definitional debate as part of the concept, not as a defect to hide.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's boilerplate framing ('Culture is a foundational concept in Anthropology... introduces its meaning, its context, and a simple way to apply it') carries no verifiable factual content and was discarded entirely.
The generated draft's claim that 'College courses use culture as a building block for later discussions, assignments, and decisions' is generic boilerplate, not a researchable claim; discarded.

sourceRecords.title: 3.1 The Homeyness of Culture — Introduction to Anthropology (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A anchor (per subject source-map). OpenStax blocks direct fetch; read via Wayback Machine capture 20220927054958 of the canonical URL. Supports: culture as the integrated combination of material objects, technologies, social relationships, everyday practices, deeply held values, and shared ideas; culture as the central concept of all four fields; the 'homeyness' of culture (one's own culture feels natural, like home); the Kabyle house example of how ideas about gender and family shape the organization of home space. Facts synthesized into original prose; lesson examples are original.

sourceRecords.title: 3.2 The Winkiness of Culture — Introduction to Anthropology (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A anchor. Read via Wayback Machine capture 20221007055647 of the canonical URL. Supports: Tylor's classic definition of culture as quoted by OpenStax; the learned/shared test (innate behaviors like blinking are biological, acquired behaviors like winking are cultural, per Clifford Geertz); enculturation as the process of acquiring culture, mostly through unconscious absorption rather than deliberate instruction; dreaming as an example of a biological process shaped by cultural meaning (Ojibwa visionary dreams). Blink/wink illustration credited to OpenStax/Geertz in the lesson; all other examples original.

sourceRecords.title: 3.3 The Elements of Culture — Introduction to Anthropology (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A anchor. Read via Wayback Machine capture 20220929132910 of the canonical URL. Supports the three categories of culture (what we make, what we do, what we think): material culture, cultural practices (routine or habitual behavior, e.g. the Istanbul carpet seller's sales strategies), cultural frames (patterned shared ways of interpreting situations), norms, values, ideologies, and worldviews. Used for the vocabulary definitions of cultural practice and cultural frame and for the material/nonmaterial distinction; lesson wording is original.

sourceRecords.title: 3.6 The Paradoxes of Culture — Introduction to Anthropology (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A anchor. Read via Wayback Machine capture 20220924024340 of the canonical URL. Supports the four paradoxes of culture (continuous but changes; bounded but mobile; consensual but contested; shared but varies), the four mechanisms of cultural change — diffusion, friction, innovation, invention — and Franz Boas's argument that cultural elements are highly mobile through trade and migration. Also supports that culture is unevenly shared within groups and that no single member fully represents a culture. Lesson examples (the river-valley rice town, the coastal town's dance practices) are original.

sourceRecords.title: Ch. 3 Key Terms — Introduction to Anthropology (OpenStax)

Vocabulary definitions in the lesson are original prose informed by this glossary.
